title: Apply remedial behavioural techniques for a horse

lessons.title: Understanding problem behaviour
lessons.html:
Why horses develop problem behaviour

Most problem behaviours are a horse's normal response to fear, pain, confusion or poor management, which have been accidentally rewarded. Before applying any training technique, find the cause.

Common causes

  • Pain: back pain from a badly fitted saddle, sharp teeth, ulcers, lameness. A horse that suddenly starts bucking or refusing may be in pain.
  • Fear: past bad experiences, such as rough loading.
  • Confusion: unclear or conflicting aids.
  • Management: too much energy feed, too little turnout, isolation from other horses.
  • Accidental reinforcement: a horse that pulls back and gets released learns that pulling back works.

Typical problem behaviours

BehaviourPossible causes
Napping, rearing, buckingPain, fear, rider confusion, herd-bound
Refusing to loadFear of the dark, small box, past bad trips
Biting, kickingPain, rough handling, food rewards, dominance learned by success
Difficult to catchCatching only for work, rough handling
Pulling back when tiedFear, earlier escape rewarded
Stereotypies (crib-biting, weaving)Stress, confinement, low forage diet

Assessment before training

  1. Get a full history from the owner.
  2. Have the vet rule out pain: teeth, back, feet, ulcers.
  3. Check tack fit, feeding and management.
  4. Observe the behaviour safely: when, where, with whom, and what happens just before and after.
  5. Write down a clear training goal, for example "Loads calmly in under five minutes."

Stereotypies are usually reduced by management changes (more forage, turnout and company), not by punishment or blocking devices.

lessons.title: Applying remedial training techniques
lessons.html:
Learning theory

Horses learn by association and consequence.

  • Negative reinforcement (pressure and release): apply light pressure and release it the instant the horse gives the right response. The release teaches. Timing is everything.
  • Positive reinforcement: add something pleasant (a scratch, a food reward, a rest) for the right response.
  • Habituation: repeated, harmless exposure until the horse stops reacting.
  • Systematic desensitisation: start with a weak form of a frightening thing at a level the horse can cope with, then gradually increase it.
  • Shaping: reward small steps towards the final behaviour.

Punishment usually increases fear and can make horses dangerous. Avoid it.

Example: remedial loading

  1. Park the horsebox safely, ramp down, partitions open, interior light on.
  2. Use a well-fitted halter and long lead rope; handler wears helmet and gloves.
  3. Ask the horse forward with light pressure; release as soon as it takes a step towards the ramp.
  4. Allow it to look and sniff. Reward each step.
  5. Repeat short sessions, ending on a good step forward.
  6. When it walks in, feed it inside and walk it out calmly. Repeat until loading is calm. Then close the partition for short periods before travelling.

Safety rules

  • Work in a safe, enclosed area with good footing.
  • Never stand directly in front of or behind the horse.
  • Never wrap ropes around hands or tie a frightened horse solidly.
  • Stop if the horse or handler is getting stressed; return to an easier step.

Monitoring and records

Record each session: date, duration, steps achieved, problems. Review progress with the owner, and teach the owner to handle the horse consistently, otherwise the old behaviour returns.

Key points

  • Find the cause first; rule out pain with the vet.
  • Negative reinforcement works through the timely release of pressure.
  • Desensitise gradually and shape small steps.
  • Avoid punishment; it increases fear.
  • Keep sessions short, safe and recorded, and coach the owner.
